rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to capture all 10 compounds and map the overall elution window without likely truncation. The wide phi range and mid-length gradient should reveal whether peaks are early, late, or compressed, guiding the next narrowing of phi window and slope.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient and the run finished far earlier than needed, so trim the gradient window to bracket the observed elution region and improve time efficiency while keeping similar slope. This should keep all peaks in-gradient and test whether the critical mid-cluster gains selectivity from a more focused phi window.

The first method already had perfect resolution and only a time penalty, so the fastest path to a better CRF is a steeper version of that broad gradient. Shortening tG should compress the chromatogram and reduce run time while checking whether the critical 6/7 region still stays comfortably resolved.

The 12 min gradient is fast enough but slightly over-compressed the critical 6/7 pair, so make a small move shallower while holding the successful phi window and temperature fixed. This should improve the minimum resolution with only a modest time increase and may beat the current CRF optimum.

The limiting pair 6/7 clearly improves as the gradient is made slightly shallower, and there is still no time penalty at 14 min. Testing 16 min maps that trend and may raise the resolution term further while likely remaining in the zero time-penalty region.

Slope tuning suggests the critical 6/7 pair is close to the optimum at 14–16 min, so the next lever is temperature to alter selectivity rather than gradient compression. A 5 C decrease should modestly change relative retention in the crowded region while likely keeping the run within the no-time-penalty window.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing the 5/6 pair, so test the opposite direction to see whether higher temperature separates the crowded center better. Keeping the otherwise near-optimal 14 min broad gradient isolates temperature as the selectivity variable.

Temperature is clearly inferior to 40 C, so continue slope mapping on-grid beyond 16 min to define the best tradeoff between the improving 6/7 resolution and emerging time penalty. This checks whether the resolution term has fully plateaued or if 16 min is already the practical optimum.

The optimum is near 14 min at 40 C, and all peaks elute far before the gradient end, so slightly narrowing the high-organic end may fine-tune selectivity in the crowded middle without sacrificing elution. This tests whether the critical pair responds to a modestly shifted phi window rather than more slope or temperature changes.

Narrowing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the CRF, so continue in the same direction to see if the crowded center gains a bit more selectivity while all compounds still elute within the gradient. This is a focused local refinement around the current best method.

With phi1 = 0.90 giving the best selectivity so far, test a slightly steeper gradient to check whether the run can be shortened further without giving up too much on the critical 6/7 pair. This probes whether the current optimum is driven more by the phi window than by the exact 14 min slope.

At phi1 = 0.90, 12 min was too steep and 14 min is excellent, so test the slightly shallower 16 min point to see whether the small gain in minimum resolution outweighs any emerging time penalty. This is the key local comparison around the current best condition.

Slope and phi-window optimization now point strongly to 0.05–0.90 over 14 min, so make one selective temperature probe below 35 C to see if a larger thermal shift can break the stubborn 6/7 pair apart. This is a higher-risk but potentially high-reward selectivity test around the current best method.

Large temperature excursions strongly reshape the crowded center, so test the opposite high side once around the best phi-window to rule out a favorable selectivity crossover above 45 C. If it also degrades the central cluster, we can confidently stop spending injections on temperature and focus only on phi-window refinement.

Temperature clearly changes the identity of the critical overlap, and one more high-temperature step can test for a narrow selectivity sweet spot beyond 50 C before abandoning temperature entirely. This is the last efficient chance to detect a favorable thermal crossover for the stubborn middle cluster.

55 C gave the best selectivity seen so far at 14 min, so now test whether that thermal advantage survives a steeper gradient and can deliver an equally strong or even better CRF with a shorter run. This isolates whether the new optimum is robust to slope around the best temperature.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this run should only check for an equally optimal but potentially more robust local variant by slightly narrowing the upper phi limit around the perfect method. If it drops, we confirm that 0.05–0.90 over 12 min at 55 C is the clear final choice.

Since 0.85 was slightly worse than the perfect 0.90 condition, test the symmetric side at phi1 = 0.95 to confirm the local optimum in phi1 around the best method. This gives a clean robustness check while staying very close to the current maximum-CRF condition.

With two distinct methods now achieving the maximum CRF, test whether a slightly higher starting organic further improves robustness and early spacing while retaining the excellent hot, steep separation. This explores the remaining local degree of freedom around the apparent optimum family.

The best family is now clearly 55 C with phi0 = 0.05 and broad upper phi, so the remaining question is whether an even steeper gradient can still stay at the CRF ceiling. Testing 10 min probes the shortest practical runtime before the critical central pair begins to collapse too much.

We already have the maximum score, so use the remaining budget to test whether the hot optimum extends to 60 C and perhaps offers an equally perfect but faster, more robust endpoint. This is the last unexplored temperature adjacent to the best-performing region.

The 10 min gradient at phi1 = 0.95 was too steep for the 4/5 pair, so slightly narrowing the gradient window may recover enough selectivity to approach the optimum at the shorter runtime. This is a final targeted attempt to see if the 10 min method can be rescued by phi-window tuning.

We already have maximum CRF, so use a remaining run to map the lower side of phi1 more aggressively around the perfect hot 12 min method and confirm where the optimum family breaks down. This helps distinguish whether the broad-window maximum is a plateau or a true local optimum.

The hot 12 min method remains excellent even as phi1 is lowered to 0.80, so take one more step down to define the lower edge of the maximum-CRF plateau. This is a near-best robustness probe around the already optimal condition family.

Use the final run to confirm that 55 C is truly the thermal optimum for the winning 12 min, broad-window method by checking the nearest lower temperature under the co-best phi/tG setting. A drop here would cleanly validate injection 18/16 as the final recommended method family.
